title: Phoenix: A Refactored I/O Stack for GPU Direct Storage without Phony Buffers
problem: GPU Direct Storage (GDS) employs phony buffers in host memory to interact with the Linux kernel, resulting in suboptimal I/O performance, extra resource consumption, and high deployment complexity.
motivation: GDS is vital for GPU-based training and inference, but current implementations use indirect buffering that adds latency and overhead. Eliminating this intermediary layer could improve data transfer efficiency and reduce complexity.
method: Phoenix leverages ZONE_DEVICE (Linux kernel 4.3+) to map GPU memory into the page table at system startup, eliminating the need for host-side phony buffers. The kernel module allocates user-space virtual memory and establishes direct mapping with designated GPU memory.
key_novelty: Direct GPU memory mapping into the system page table using ZONE_DEVICE, eliminating intermediate host buffers while maintaining kernel compatibility.
contributions: 70.3% reduction in software processing overhead along the critical I/O path
2.29x improvement in small-size I/O performance (e.g., KV-cache operations)
4.11x improvement in large file loading performance (e.g., checkpoint loading)
Implementation for recently-released GPU and NPU models
baselines: State-of-the-art GDS I/O stack (with phony buffers)
limitations: Full-text not available; analysis based on abstract. Evaluation may be limited to specific GPU models.
primary_theme: GPU-centric I/O optimization for AI/ML workloads
